faq.title: Questions students ask us.
faq.lede: Can't find your answer? Our guides go deeper, with sources.

free.a: Searching universities, checking basic eligibility and reading guides are free. Paid services such as document review or a dedicated counselor are optional, and their prices are shown in the app for your region before you buy.

visa.a: No. Visas are decided by the Korean immigration authorities and diplomatic missions. Hangyul helps you prepare a complete application and track each step.

agency.q: Do I have to work with an agency?
agency.a: No. You can explore, match and prepare on your own. A partner agency is assigned only if you choose a support service.

tuition.q: Who do I pay tuition to?
tuition.a: Always directly to the university, in your own name, through the university's payment channel. Hangyul never collects tuition on a university's behalf.

languages.q: Is the site available in my language?
languages.a: The site is available in many languages. English and Korean are reviewed. Languages marked β are machine-translated and awaiting review, and guides are shown in English where no translation exists.

prices.q: Why don't you show prices on this page?
prices.a: Prices depend on your region and currency, so we show them in the app before you buy, never after.

trust.title: Every fact has a source and a date.
trust.lede: Study-abroad rules change often: apostille memberships, visa thresholds, deadlines. Here's how we keep what you read accurate, and the full list of sources we rely on.

source.title: Linked to a source
source.text: Requirements, deadlines and rules link to the official page or document they come from.

date.title: Dated and time-versioned
date.text: Rules that change on a known date, such as a country joining the Apostille Convention, are stored with that date.

review.title: Reviewed on a schedule
review.text: Each source has a review interval. When it's overdue or changes, the affected information is flagged for review.

demo.title: Unverified means labelled
demo.text: Anything we haven't verified against an official source says so, with the date we last checked.

statusText.CURRENT: Checked within its review interval and unchanged.
statusText.REVIEW_DUE: Due for a re-check. The information is still shown, with this label.
statusText.CHANGED: The source changed since we last checked; affected information is being reviewed.

trust.registryLede: Government bodies, official portals, universities and reputable news, each with its status and the date it was last checked.
trust.footnote: Official sources always take precedence over anything shown on Hangyul Univ. Follow the links to check the original.

faq.title: What students actually ask us.
faq.lede: Short answers. Every number on this site links to the source it came from and the day we checked it.

topik.q: Do I need TOPIK to apply?
topik.a: Not always. English-taught degrees accept IELTS or TOEFL instead, and university Korean language programmes accept you with no test at all. The quick check above counts how many programmes in our catalogue accept the level you have today.

noKorean.q: Can I go to Korea without speaking Korean?
noKorean.a: Yes. Most students start at a university's Korean language institute on a D-4-1 visa and move to a degree and a D-2 visa once they reach the level that degree asks for, usually TOPIK level 3. English-taught degrees are the other route and ask for IELTS or TOEFL instead.

documents.a: Usually a diploma, transcripts, a passport, a bank certificate and a personal statement, plus an apostille or consular legalization depending on which country issued them. Each university publishes its own list; we show that list on the programme page with the date we last checked it.

cost.q: How much does the first year cost?
cost.a: Every programme card shows a first-year figure built from tuition, the application fee and estimated living costs. While Hangyul is still verifying the catalogue, those figures are sample data and are labelled as such. The programme page always shows where a number came from.

scholarship.a: Yes: university scholarships, government scholarships, and reductions tied to your TOPIK level. The programme page lists the ones that programme publishes, with the source. We never estimate an award you might get.

age.a: Universities rarely publish a hard limit, but many ask how long it has been since you last graduated and expect an explanation for a long gap. Where a programme publishes a rule about it, we show the rule.

deadline.a: Most intakes close three to six months before the semester begins, and the visa adds one to two more months after admission. A year ahead is comfortable; six months is tight but possible if your documents are already legalized.

work.q: Can I work while I study?
work.a: On a D-2 visa you can apply for part-time work permission, normally after your first semester and within hours set by immigration. It is permission you apply for, not something the visa gives you automatically.

q1.q: Which documents do I need to apply?
q1.a:
These are the documents needed for admission. Some universities and departments ask for more, and you can also submit recommendation letters from teachers or employers, or a certificate of olympiad participation.

1. * High school or junior college graduation certificate, translated into English, notarized and apostilled
2. Academic transcript, translated into English, notarized and apostilled
3. Copy of your passport
4. Copies of both parents' passports. If a parent has no passport, a copy of their ID card, translated into English and notarized
5. Birth certificate or family relationship certificate, translated and notarized
6. Proof of Korean or English ability (TOPIK, TOEFL, IELTS or equivalent evidence)
7. Bank balance certificate showing USD 15,000 or more, valid for 30 days (the amount can vary with the university's location)

q2.q: Do I need a TOPIK score?
q2.a: Most Korean universities ask for a Korean or English test result (TOPIK, TOEFL or IELTS). Some also accept their own Korean-language test instead.

q3.a: Universities accept TOPIK, TOEFL and IELTS. Some also accept a certificate from a university's Korean language institute in Korea, a pass in the university's own Korean test, or a King Sejong Institute certificate at intermediate level 1 or above.

q4.q: Can I apply if I don't speak Korean?
q4.a: Yes. On an English-taught program you can study entirely in English.

q5.a: They depend on the university and the program. We recommend starting at least six months before your course begins so there is time to prepare your documents. Language courses usually need less lead time.

q6.q: Which universities offer scholarships to international students?
q6.a: Most do, but the amounts and the conditions differ from one university to another.

q7.a: There is no minimum grade to apply to a Korean university, but higher grades give you a better chance at the universities you want.

q8.a: Most Korean universities have no age limit, though a few do. If that applies to you, we can suggest universities where age is not an issue. Either way you need a high-school or junior-college graduation certificate.

q9.q: Can I start university straight after high school?
q9.a: Yes. You can apply to a Korean university as soon as you graduate from high school or junior college.

q10.q: Is it easy to find a job in Korea after graduating?
q10.a: It depends on your field. Graduates in engineering and business usually find work more easily than graduates in the humanities.

terms.intro: Hangyul Univ helps people preparing to study in Korea look up university information, get their documents and application steps ready, and use services such as consultations, essay editing and application management.

purpose.p: These terms set out the basic matters between Hangyul and members in connection with the use of the Hangyul Univ service.

service.def: The Hangyul Univ website and mobile apps, and the study-abroad preparation and application features provided through them.

member.def: A person who has agreed to these terms, created an account and uses the service.

support.def: The paid services a member chooses, such as consultations, document review, editing of personal statements and study plans, and application management.

agency.def: A study-abroad agency under contract with Hangyul that carries out consultations and document work for a member.

university.def: The Korean higher-education institution a member applies to.

content.def: University information, guidance and forms that Hangyul has produced or collected and that the service provides.

accounts.p: Members must give accurate information when registering and when using the service. An account may be used only by the person it belongs to, and may not be transferred or lent to anyone else without Hangyul’s agreement. If there are signs that an account has been compromised, Hangyul will suspend it to protect the member and tell them.

services.documents: Help preparing application documents, and document review
services.writing: Editing of personal statements and study plans
services.applications: Preparing and managing university applications with you
services.visa: Guidance on preparing your visa documents
services.scope: What is actually provided in any one case depends on the product or plan the member chose, and is shown on that product’s own page before purchase.

universityInfo.p: University information in the service is based on published sources: Korea's official university disclosure service (Academy Info), Study in Korea, and each university's own official material. Information that changes between intakes is shown with its source and the date it was checked. Public university pages are for information; what you are eligible for, and what you need to prepare, is shown in the student platform after you sign in.

support.coordination: Hangyul coordinates the member's whole preparation process and keeps track of each step.
support.agency: Individual tasks, such as consultations, document review and preparing a submission, may be carried out by the partner agency assigned to the member.
support.responsible: The service shows who is responsible for the work at each stage.
support.decisions: Final decisions on admission, scholarships and immigration are made by each university or the relevant authority, according to their own criteria and assessment.

duties.p: Members must submit information and documents that are true. Members must not impersonate another person, submit forged or altered documents, misuse accounts, interfere with the proper operation of the service, or infringe the rights of others.

fees.shown: The price of a paid service and what it includes are shown on that product’s page before payment, and nothing is charged beyond the amount shown.
fees.provider: Card details are entered on Hangyul's payment screen and passed through Hangyul's server to the payment provider (Toss Payments) for approval. Once payment completes, the transaction appears in your account.
fees.tuition: Hangyul does not collect university tuition. Tuition is paid directly to the university, in the member’s own name.

refunds.route: Cancellation and refund of a paid service can be requested from the transaction records in your account, and the person handling it will tell you the outcome.
refunds.visaRefusal: If a visa is refused after tuition has been paid, the basis and amount of any tuition refund follow that university’s refund rules. The refund is received into an account in the member’s own name.
refunds.statutory: Rights of withdrawal and refund given to consumers by the Act on Consumer Protection in Electronic Commerce and other applicable law apply regardless of these terms.
refunds.withdrawal: You may withdraw within 7 days of receiving the order confirmation (the written contract terms). If the service starts later than that, within 7 days of the day it starts. (Act on Consumer Protection in Electronic Commerce, Art. 17(1))
refunds.commenced: Once the service has started, withdrawal may be restricted. You may still withdraw for the parts of the plan that have not yet started. The service is deemed to have started when the first consultation takes place. (Art. 17(2)5)
refunds.nonConforming: If the service differs from what was advertised or agreed, you may withdraw within 3 months of receiving it or within 30 days of learning of the difference. (Art. 17(3))
refunds.effect: On withdrawal Hangyul refunds within 3 business days of the withdrawal date, paying statutory late interest for any delay, and asks the card company to cancel the charge without delay. No penalty or damages are charged for a statutory withdrawal. (Art. 18)
refunds.stagesIntro: The statutory position at each service stage:

stage.ESSAY_REVIEW_DELIVERED: Essay or study plan review delivered
stage.SETTLEMENT_STARTED: Visa, arrival and settlement support started

refunds.commercial: Hangyul’s refund schedule after the 7-day period (how delivered consultations and reviews are deducted) is set in a separate refund policy; until it is published, only the statutory rules above apply.

privacy.p: What personal information Hangyul processes, why, for how long, who it is disclosed to and what rights you have are set out in the <privacy>privacy policy</privacy>.

ip.p: Rights in content Hangyul has produced for the service belong to Hangyul or to the rightful rights holder. Rights in university names, marks and images and in other third-party material belong to their respective holders, and their appearance in the service does not by itself indicate any relationship between Hangyul and that institution.

changes.h: Changes to and suspension of the service
changes.p: Hangyul may change or discontinue parts of the service in order to improve it. Where a change or discontinuation affects the scope of a service a member has already bought, Hangyul will tell the member beforehand and refund the part of what they paid that has not been provided. Where the service is interrupted by maintenance or a fault, Hangyul will give notice as far as it reasonably can.

termination.p: Hangyul may restrict or terminate an account where a member submits forged or altered documents, impersonates another person, uses someone else’s account without authorization, or deliberately interferes with the operation of the service. Hangyul will tell the member the reason and the basis and give them an opportunity to respond; where urgent action is needed, it will tell them immediately afterwards.

liability.p: Hangyul is liable under applicable law for loss caused to a member by its intent or negligence in providing the service. Rights given to members by consumer-protection law are not limited by these terms. If a dispute arises, Hangyul and the member will first try to resolve it by discussion, and the member may apply for mediation to a dispute-resolution body such as the Korea Consumer Agency.

Seoul.line: Half of Korea's research universities are within an hour of each other here.
Seoul.body:
Seoul puts about a quarter of the country's population into one metropolitan area, and most of its best-known universities into a handful of neighborhoods: Sinchon, Anam, Gwanak and Heukseok. The subway runs until roughly midnight and a student fare across the city is about 1,500 won, so where you live and where you study do not have to be the same district.
It is the most expensive place in Korea to rent and the easiest to find part-time work, English-language services, and other people from your own country.

Gyeonggi.line: The province around Seoul: cheaper, roomier, and still on the same subway map.
Gyeonggi.body:
Gyeonggi wraps around Seoul and holds more universities than any other region except the capital itself. Suwon, Yongin, Seongnam and Bucheon are all 40–70 minutes from central Seoul on the metro or a direct bus, and rent is routinely a third less.
Campuses here tend to be larger and more self-contained than Seoul's, so more students live in university dormitories instead of off-campus studios.

Incheon.line: Korea's gateway city: the airport is in it, and so is Songdo.
Incheon.body:
Incheon is where you will land. It is also a university city in its own right: Songdo International Business District was built from reclaimed land in the last twenty years and now holds several campuses, including the Korean branches of foreign universities.
The airport railway puts central Seoul within an hour, and Incheon's old quarter (Chinatown, the port, Wolmido) feels like a different city from the new district.

Busan.line: A port city of three and a half million, built along the sea and into the hills.
Busan.body:
Busan is Korea's second-largest city and does not feel like a smaller Seoul. The universities sit between beaches and mountains, the subway reaches most of them, and rent runs well below the capital.
It has the country's largest port, a long-standing film festival, and a summer that the rest of Korea travels to. Winters are the mildest on the mainland.

Daegu.line: An inland city in a basin of mountains, known for textiles, medicine and heat.
Daegu.body:
Daegu sits in a bowl in the south-east and is the hottest city in Korea in August and one of the coldest in January. It has a dense, walkable center, a long textile history that became a fashion and medical-device industry, and a cost of living noticeably below Seoul or Busan.
The KTX puts Seoul within an hour and three quarters and Busan within fifty minutes.

Daejeon.line: Korea's science city: research institutes, engineering campuses and a lot of laboratories.
Daejeon.body:
Daejeon was built up around Daedeok Innopolis, a cluster of government research institutes and corporate R&D centers, and the universities here are shaped by it. If you are coming for engineering or the natural sciences, this is where the laboratories are.
It is almost exactly in the middle of the country: an hour from Seoul by KTX and an hour from Busan.

Gwangju.line: The cultural and political center of the south-west, and an affordable place to study.
Gwangju.body:
Gwangju is the largest city in the Jeolla provinces and carries their reputation for food and for the 1980 democratic uprising, which is still the thing the city is best known for in Korea.
It is one of the cheaper metropolitan cities to live in, has a well-regarded arts scene, and is about two hours from Seoul on the KTX.

Ulsan.line: Korea's industrial capital: shipbuilding, cars and petrochemicals.
Ulsan.body:
Ulsan has the highest average income of any Korean city, and the reason is easy to see: the world's largest shipyard, a car plant that is a district on its own, and a petrochemical complex along the coast. Engineering graduates are hired here.
It is a small city by Korean standards, half an hour from Busan, with whale-watching, a long beach and the Taehwa river running through the center.

Sejong.line: A city built from nothing since 2012 to hold the government ministries.
Sejong.body:
Sejong is Korea's newest city and the most deliberately planned: most of the central ministries moved here from Seoul, and the street layout, the parks and the public buildings all date from the last fifteen years.
It is small, quiet and extremely new, twenty minutes from Daejeon and an hour and a half from Seoul.

Gangwon.line: Mountains and the east coast: the least dense and most scenic province.
Gangwon.body:
Gangwon holds the Taebaek range, the 2018 Winter Olympics venues and the beaches of the east coast. Chuncheon, Gangneung and Wonju are the university towns; none of them is large, and all of them are cheaper and quieter than anywhere in the capital region.
Winters here are real winters. The KTX reaches Gangneung from Seoul in about two hours.

Chungbuk.line: Landlocked, central, and built around Cheongju.
Chungbuk.body:
North Chungcheong is the only Korean province with no coastline. Cheongju is its center and its main university city, close enough to both Sejong and Daejeon to share their job market.
The province is known for Danyang's limestone scenery and for a quieter, cheaper student life than the metropolitan cities offer.

Chungnam.line: Between Seoul and the south. Cheonan and Asan are a commuter-train ride from the capital.
Chungnam.body:
South Chungcheong runs from the west coast inland, and its university towns, Cheonan and Asan, are on the Seoul metro's line 1 as well as the KTX. That combination of capital-region access and provincial rent is why several large universities built campuses here.
Gongju and Buyeo, the old Baekje capitals, are in the same province and worth the afternoon.

Jeonbuk.line: Jeonju, and the region known as the home of Korean food.
Jeonbuk.body:
North Jeolla is agricultural, flat in the west and mountainous in the east, and Jeonju is its center: a city of about 650,000 with the largest surviving hanok quarter in the country and a food reputation no other Korean city disputes.
Living costs are among the lowest of any university city, and Seoul is a little under two hours by KTX.

Jeonnam.line: The south-west coast, its islands, and the slowest pace in the country.
Jeonnam.body:
South Jeolla has more islands than the rest of Korea combined, the Suncheon Bay wetlands, and Yeosu's harbor. It is the least urban of the mainland provinces and the universities here are correspondingly small and close-knit.
If you want a quiet place with a coastline and very low living costs, this is it.

Gyeongbuk.line: Gyeongju's thousand years of history and Pohang's steel, in the same province.
Gyeongbuk.body:
North Gyeongsang holds Gyeongju, the Silla capital for a millennium and effectively an open-air museum, and Pohang, a steel city that also hosts one of Korea's strongest science and engineering universities. Andong, further inland, is the center of Korean Confucian tradition.
It is a large, varied province, and all of it is cheaper than the capital region.

Gyeongnam.line: The industrial south coast: Changwon's factories and Tongyeong's harbors.
Gyeongnam.body:
South Gyeongsang wraps around Busan and shares its economy: machinery and shipbuilding in Changwon and Geoje, aerospace in Sacheon, and a coastline of fishing ports and islands further west.
Jinju and Changwon are the main university cities. Busan is never more than an hour away.

Jeju.line: A volcanic island off the south coast, and a different climate from the rest of Korea.
Jeju.body:
Jeju is 85 kilometers from the mainland, built around the Hallasan volcano, and warm enough that the vegetation looks subtropical. It is a holiday destination for the rest of the country, which shapes its economy and its rents.
There are few universities here and they are small. Flights to Seoul run every few minutes and take an hour.
